items.q: Layered (n-tier) architecture: pros/cons?
items.a:
Layers: controller → service → repository → DB, dependencies point downward.

- [[g:Pros]]: familiar, simple, easy to onboard
- [[r:Cons]]: business logic easily leaks into a thin service (anemic domain), framework/DB seeps back upward, hard to test logic in isolation, prone to becoming a 'big ball of mud' as it grows

:::deep
- dependencies point *downward* to the DB → framework/JPA/DB seeps back up into the domain (JPA entity = domain model → tight coupling to infrastructure)
- business logic leaks into a thin 'service' → [[r:anemic domain]] (entity is just getters/setters); prone to becoming a 'big ball of mud' (god-class service)

[[o:Layered is NOT wrong]] — it's a reasonable default for most apps; it only becomes a problem when the domain is complex & long-lived (fintech core). That's when you move to Hexagonal/Clean. [[r:Don't over-engineer Clean for simple CRUD.]]

- The clearest sign layered has run out of room: when a small business change forces edits across all four layers, or when testing one business rule requires standing up the whole Spring context plus a database. The real-world build of the replacement architecture is in 12.15, and the gradual migration path is in 12.21.
:::

items.q: Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters): what's the core idea?
items.a: Put [[g:the domain at the center]], communicating outward through a [[b:port]] (interface). The outside world (web, DB, queue) is an [[b:adapter]] plugged into the port. The domain [[r:knows NOTHING]] about the framework/DB. - [[b:driving adapter]] (UI/API): calls *into* the domain - [[b:driven adapter]] (DB/broker): is called *out* to by the domain through a port Benefit: swapping infrastructure doesn't touch the domain, the domain can be tested with mock adapters, boundaries are clear. :::deep - the domain defines the port (interface); the adapter implements the port (dependency inversion: the domain defines `PaymentGateway`, infrastructure implements a Stripe adapter) - measurable benefit: test the use case with an in-memory adapter (no DB/Docker), swap infrastructure without touching the domain OTA: the Booking domain doesn't know about Postgres/Kafka/GDS — it has ports `SeatInventory`, `PaymentGateway`, `GdsClient`; adapters plug into them. [[r:The cost]]: mapping between domain entities and JPA + a lot of interfaces → only worth it when the domain is complex. - The real-world build in code: `port/in`, `port/out` package structure, adapters for a Spring Boot service (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q1), and which layer transaction/validation/mapping belong in (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q5). :::

items.q: Clean Architecture and the Dependency Rule?
items.a:
Concentric rings: Entities → Use Cases → Interface Adapters → Frameworks/Drivers.

[[g:Dependency Rule]]: dependencies point *inward* only; an inner ring never knows about an outer ring.

Uses [[g:dependency inversion]] (interface on the inside, implementation on the outside) → DB/web become swappable details.

:::tip Bottom line
Hexagonal, Onion, and Clean are the same idea: domain at the core, infrastructure at the edge, dependencies pointing inward. They differ mostly in vocabulary and level of detail.
:::

:::deep
- Clean/Hexagonal is NOT 'split into 4 folders' — it's a [[g:dependency rule]] — the domain imports nothing from Spring/JPA/Kafka
- enforced through dependency inversion: the domain defines `PaymentGateway` (a port), the infrastructure module implements it with a Stripe/PSP adapter
- benefit: test the use case with an in-memory adapter, swap the PSP without touching the domain, the domain reads as pure 'business' with no 'JPA' in sight

[[r:The cost]]: lots of interfaces/mapping — only worth it when the domain is complex. Plain CRUD → layered is enough. Bottom line: 'architecture serves the business's rate of change, not diagram aesthetics'.

- The real-world build: package structure for a Spring Boot service (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q1), and enforcing the Dependency Rule with ArchUnit or Spring Modulith instead of relying on a promise (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q4) — without tooling the dependency rule drifts within a few months.
:::

items.q: Layered vs Hexagonal/Clean — when to pick which?
items.a:
LayeredHexagonal/Clean
Good fit forsimple CRUD, small team, thin domaincomplex domain, long lifespan, many integrations
Testabilitytied to DB/frameworktest the domain with a mock adapter
Changing infrastructureseeps everywhereonly touch the adapter
Costlowmore layers/abstraction
:::warn Warning don't apply Clean to trivial CRUD — the boilerplate cost isn't worth it. Choose based on domain complexity. ::: :::deep - [[o:not a whole-system binary choice]] — apply it *per service/context*: complex Booking/Payment → Clean; simple lookup/reporting → layered - signs you need Clean: logic is hard to test because it's tied to DB/framework, or swapping a PSP means editing everywhere - signs of over-engineering: lots of interfaces/mapping for trivial CRUD 'Architecture serves the business's rate of change, not diagram aesthetics' — choose based on domain complexity & how often it changes. - Measure the cost and the benefit with the test pyramid mapped onto each layer (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q6); migrating a running layered codebase gradually follows the six steps in 12.21. :::

items.q: Strategic DDD: bounded context, ubiquitous language, context mapping?
items.a:
- [[b:Bounded Context]]: a boundary within which one model/language has consistent meaning ('Account' in Billing differs from Auth) → a natural choice for micro-service boundaries
- [[b:Ubiquitous Language]]: developers and domain experts share the same vocabulary, reflected in the code
- [[b:Context Mapping]]: describes the relationships between contexts (Customer-Supplier, Anti-Corruption Layer, Shared Kernel...)

:::tip Bottom line
Strategic DDD is essentially the tool for [[g:drawing micro-service boundaries]] along business lines — matching 'service boundary = consistency boundary'.
:::

:::deep
- a bounded context is usually = one service + one dedicated DB; the boundary sits where language/meaning changes (OTA: 'Booking', 'Inventory', 'Pricing', 'Payment', 'Loyalty' — 'fare' in Pricing differs from 'amount' in Payment)
- context map: Payment = Supplier, Booking = Customer; insert an *Anti-Corruption Layer* when integrating a legacy GDS
- an aggregate holds invariants within a transaction boundary (`Booking` guarantees 'total seats = number of passengers')

[[r:Mistake]]: splitting services by technical layer (controller-service-dao) instead of by business capability → distributed monolith.

- Topic 24 is the deep dive on this section: getting the ubiquitous language right (24-domain-driven-design.strategic-splitting-the-domain.q1), finding boundaries with event storming (24-domain-driven-design.strategic-splitting-the-domain.q4), and the relationship types in a context map (24-domain-driven-design.strategic-splitting-the-domain.q3).
:::

items.q: Tactical DDD: entity, value object, aggregate, repository, domain event?
items.a:
- [[b:Entity]]: has identity, a lifecycle (Account, Order)
- [[b:Value Object]]: immutable, defined by its value (Money, Address)
- [[b:Aggregate]]: a cluster of objects with an *aggregate root* as the entry point, protecting invariants; a transaction should be scoped to one aggregate
- [[b:Repository]]: an abstraction for retrieving aggregates (hides the DB)
- [[b:Domain Event]]: something that already happened (OrderPlaced) — the foundation for event-driven/outbox

[[g:Money]] is the classic value object in fintech (immutable, carries a currency).

:::deep
- an [[g:Aggregate]] is a *transaction & consistency* boundary — only changed through the *aggregate root*, protecting invariants; one transaction should be scoped to *one* aggregate (cross-aggregate work uses eventual consistency + domain events)
- keep aggregates small ([[r:don't gather the whole world]] → heavy contention/locking)
- Value Objects are immutable (Money, SeatNumber) — compared by value, thread-safe

OTA: the `Booking` aggregate holds the seat/price invariant; `LedgerEntry` is append-only; a `PaymentSucceeded` domain event is published. [[r:An aggregate boundary that's too large = lock contention & hard to scale.]]

- Deep dive into each block: Entity vs. Value Object (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q1), how to size aggregate boundaries (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q2), where Repository/Factory/Domain Service each belong (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q4).
:::

items.q: When SHOULD and SHOULDN'T you use DDD?
items.a:
- [[g:Use it]] when the domain is *business-complex* (many rules, changing over time) — fintech, insurance, logistics
- [[r:Don't]] when it's just CRUD/forms-over-data: the conceptual cost (aggregate, context) > the benefit

DDD is about *modelling the business*, not a mandatory code pattern.

:::deep
- USE it when the domain is complex (many rules, needs a shared language with domain experts) — fintech, OTA (fare rules, overbooking, refund policy)
- DON'T when it's CRUD/forms-over-data (the cost of aggregates, bounded contexts, mapping > the benefit)
- you can use strategic DDD (bounded contexts splitting services) without heavy tactical DDD, or vice versa

[[o:Apply DDD selectively]]: core domain (booking/pricing/ledger: full tactical DDD) vs. supporting/generic (notifications/reporting: layered/CRUD or buy off-the-shelf). [[r:Mistake]]: DDD-ifying everything, or skipping it on a genuinely complex core (anemic domain + logic leaking through every service).

- 'What problem DDD actually solves' is covered in more depth in 24.1 — and it also opens with exactly this question of when not to use it.
:::

items.q: CQRS and Event Sourcing — when do they make sense?
items.a:
- [[b:CQRS]]: separates the write model (command) from the read model (query) → each optimized independently, reads use a read model/projection
- [[b:Event Sourcing]]: state = a sequence of events

A powerful pairing for audit trails & rebuilding views (a great fit for a ledger).

[[r:Trade-off]]: complexity, eventual consistency between the write and read model, event versioning.

[[o:Don't use it by default]] — only when audit needs/read scaling/model transformation justify it.

:::deep
- CQRS separates the command (normalized, protects invariants) from the query (read model optimized for the screen) → scale & optimize independently; the read model can be denormalized/live in a different store (Elasticsearch/Redis)
- Event Sourcing stores the event sequence as the source of truth → perfect audit trail, time-travel, rebuildable projections
- trade-offs: eventual consistency between write↔read model, event versioning/upcasting, snapshots for fast replay

OTA: an event-sourced ledger (easy reconciliation/balance rebuilding); a separate 'booking history' read model projection. But [[g:lightweight CQRS]] (just splitting the read model, not full ES) is usually enough — don't default to full ES because it 'sounds impressive'.

- Before even considering event sourcing, distinguish a domain event from an integration event first (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3): using domain events doesn't mean storing state as events.
:::

items.q: Which design patterns should a senior engineer know cold (and why)?
items.a:
- [[b:Strategy]]: pick an algorithm at runtime (PSP routing) — avoids a giant if-else chain
- [[b:Factory/Abstract Factory]]: create complex/multi-variant objects
- [[b:Builder]]: construct an immutable object with many fields
- [[b:Decorator]]: add behavior (logging, caching) without modifying the core
- [[b:Adapter]]: bridge incompatible interfaces (anti-corruption layer)
- [[b:Observer]]: internal event-driven behavior
- distributed: Circuit Breaker, Saga, Outbox, CQRS

[[o:Describe a pattern through the *problem* + *trade-off*, not just the name.]]

:::deep
- Strategy (routing PSP/GDS by condition, replacing if-else — underpins OCP), Factory (multi-variant objects)
- Builder (immutable object with many fields — Itinerary), Decorator (logging/caching/retry without touching the core), Adapter (ACL with a legacy GDS), Observer (internal event-driven behavior)

A pattern is *shared vocabulary* + a proven solution — but [[r:don't cram patterns in]] (over-engineering); pick one when the problem genuinely shows up. Knowing when NOT to use a pattern matters just as much for a senior engineer.
:::

items.q: SOLID — a pragmatic reading for backend engineers?
items.a:
- [[b:S]]RP: a class has one reason to change
- [[b:O]]CP: open for extension, closed for modification (Strategy/polymorphism)
- [[b:L]]SP: a subtype can replace its supertype without breaking behavior
- [[b:I]]SP: small, need-specific interfaces, avoid a 'fat interface'
- [[b:D]]IP: depend on abstractions — the foundation of Hexagonal/Clean

[[g:DIP + ISP]] are exactly what let the domain stay independent of infrastructure.

:::deep
- SRP: a service/class shouldn't carry multiple responsibilities (PaymentService shouldn't also do notifications)
- OCP: adding a new PSP shouldn't require editing existing code (Strategy/polymorphism)
- LSP: don't override in a way that narrows behavior; ISP: small need-specific interfaces (avoid a fat interface); DIP: the domain defines the port, infrastructure implements it

[[o:SOLID is guidance, not hard law]] — apply it with judgment ([[r:don't create an abstraction for something with only one implementation 'just in case']] → YAGNI). The goal: code that's safe to change, not dogma compliance.
:::

items.q: Common anti-patterns: distributed monolith, anemic domain, god object?
items.a:
- [[r:Distributed monolith]]: services are split but tightly coupled (shared DB, long synchronous call chains) → you get all of micro-services' downsides with none of the benefits. Sign: changing 1 service forces deploying several others
- [[r:Anemic domain model]]: entities are just getters/setters, logic piles up in the service → loses the power of OOP/DDD
- [[r:God object/service]]: one class does far too much

:::warn Golden rule
'a service does not share a database'. Two services writing to the same table is a distributed-monolith red flag.
:::

:::deep
- [[r:Distributed monolith]]: tight coupling (shared DB, long synchronous call chains, synchronized deploys). Sign: changing 1 service forces deploying 5 others; two services writing to the same table → fix: database-per-service, clear async communication/contracts, boundaries drawn along bounded contexts
- Anemic domain → fix: move behavior/invariants into the aggregate; God object → fix: split along SRP

'Micro-services are a trade-off, not an upgrade'; without a clear organizational/scaling reason → stick with a [[g:modular monolith]].

- Anemic domain from the DDD angle: how to spot it (24-domain-driven-design.strategic-splitting-the-domain.q1) and how to avoid it — behavior belongs to the aggregate, and only what belongs to no aggregate becomes a Domain Service (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q4).
:::

items.q: Coupling & cohesion — the design compass?
items.a:
Goal: [[g:low coupling, high cohesion]] — independent modules, each module gathering related things. - low coupling → local changes don't spread - high cohesion → code is easy to understand/locate This is the implicit criterion behind every module/service boundary decision.
Coupling typeSymptomDanger level
Shared databasetwo services write to the same tablehighest — nobody can change the schema anymore
Long synchronous call chainsA calls B calls C calls Dhigh — errors and latency compound
Shared model libraryone shared DTO jarmedium — bumping the version touches everyone
Via events with a contractpublish/subscribelow — but still needs versioning
:::deep - low coupling = changing A doesn't force changing B (via interface/event, not sharing internals/DB) - high cohesion = everything in a module serves one purpose - measure by: how far do changes spread? (high coupling = spreads a lot); does a module have 'many reasons to change'? (low cohesion) A bounded context = a cohesion boundary; coupling between contexts is kept minimal via context map/ACL/events. [[o:Connascence]] (how strongly two parts must change together) is a more refined way to measure coupling. Bottom line: two things that must change together often → same module; loosely related → split apart. :::

items.q: Modular monolith vs micro-services — when do you split?
items.a:
Modular monolithMicro-services
Deploysingleeach service independently
Transactionlocal ACIDdistributed (Saga)
Operationssimplenetwork, consistency, observability
Split when—need independent scale/deploy/team
:::tip 8 years of experience, bottom line start with a modular monolith with clean boundaries; only split into micro-services when there's a clear organizational/scaling reason. 'Microservices are a trade-off, not an upgrade.' ::: :::deep - [[b:Modular monolith]]: single deploy, clearly bounded modules (each module has an internal API, no reaching across internals) → 1 deploy, schema-per-module, local ACID transactions, boundaries are easy to refactor (same codebase) - [[b:Micro-services]] when you need: independent scaling, independent deploys per team (Conway's law), isolating failures/technology — traded for distributed complexity Start with a modular monolith with clean boundaries (easy to split later); split when there's a clear *organizational/scaling* reason. [[r:Splitting too early + wrong boundaries = distributed monolith.]] - Enforcing module boundaries right inside the monolith with Spring Modulith, and package-by-feature vs. package-by-layer (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q8). :::

items.q: What does an Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) do when integrating with a legacy system?
items.a:
[[g:ACL]] (Anti-Corruption Layer) = a translation layer between your domain and an external/legacy system with a different model → protects the domain from being 'contaminated' by bad concepts/structures.

- usually implemented as an Adapter + mapping
- useful when integrating with old core banking systems or a PSP with a non-standard model

:::warn Interview trap
An ACL is easily mistaken for 'just a mapper'. The distinguishing point: a mapper translates *structure* (this field to that field), while an ACL also translates *concepts* — the other side calls it `PAX` with five states while your domain only has three, and the ACL must decide which mapping applies and reject what's invalid. If your ACL never throws an error anywhere, it's almost certainly just a mapper.
:::

:::deep
- ACL = Adapter + mapping between the domain and a messy external/legacy system → changes on their side only affect the ACL, never spreading into the domain
- implementation: an interface (port) on the domain side + an adapter that translates the external system's DTO ↔ the domain model, also handling differences in semantics/units/errors

OTA: integrating a legacy GDS/airline system (Amadeus/Sabre with their own schema/format, odd error codes) through an ACL → the Booking domain only ever sees a clean model; switching GDS providers only touches the ACL.

The ACL is also where you gather retry/idempotency/circuit-breaker logic for external integrations.

- ACL is one relationship type in a context map, alongside Customer/Supplier, Conformist, and Open Host Service — pick the wrong relationship type and an ACL can't save you (24-domain-driven-design.strategic-splitting-the-domain.q3).
:::

sections.title: Clean & layered — building it for real

items.q: What does a real-world package structure for a Spring Boot service look like under Clean/Hexagonal?
items.a:
12.3 covers the *rule*; this one covers the *folders*. The most common structure, split by [[g:feature first, layer second]]: 
com.acme.booking
├── domain/                     // does NOT import Spring, JPA, Jackson
│   ├── Booking.java            // business entity + invariants
│   ├── Money.java              // value object
│   ├── BookingStatus.java
│   └── DomainException.java
├── application/
│   ├── port/in/                // use case interface (entry port)
│   │   ├── HoldSeatUseCase.java
│   │   └── CancelBookingUseCase.java
│   ├── port/out/               // exit port — domain DEFINES it, infrastructure implements it
│   │   ├── BookingRepository.java
│   │   ├── PaymentGateway.java
│   │   └── SeatLockPort.java
│   └── service/
│       └── HoldSeatService.java   // orchestration, opens the transaction
├── adapter/
│   ├── in/web/                 // Controller, request/response DTOs
│   ├── in/messaging/           // Kafka consumer
│   ├── out/persistence/        // JpaBookingRepository + BookingJpaEntity
│   └── out/psp/                // StripePaymentGateway
└── config/                     // @Configuration, wiring, the only place that knows everything
Dependency direction: `adapter` → `application` → `domain`. [[r:Never the other way around.]] An easily missed point: [[o:`port/out` lives inside `application`, not inside `adapter`]]. The interface is defined by the inside according to its own needs, and the outside is what implements it — that's exactly dependency inversion, and it's also what separates someone who understands it from someone who just copied the folder layout. :::deep - Name ports after the [[g:business language]], not the technology: `PaymentGateway`, not `StripeClient`; `SeatLockPort`, not `RedisLock`. A name that leaks the technology is a sign infrastructure is seeping inward. - one use case = one small interface in `port/in` (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q3). A 20-method interface is the old `Service` wearing a new outfit. - `config` is the [[o:only place]] allowed to know about every layer — it wires adapters into ports. Keep it thin and free of logic. - package-private is your friend: keeping `BookingJpaEntity` package-private inside `out/persistence` means no other layer can accidentally use it (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q8). - [[r:Don't]] create a separate Maven module right from the start — use packages first, split into modules only when you genuinely need to enforce the boundary (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q4). - For a thin domain (CRUD), this structure is over-engineering — 12.4 already warned about this. Use it when the domain has real invariants worth protecting. :::

items.q: Domain model and JPA entity: two separate classes, or share one class?
How should a use case (application service) be designed? One class per use case, or grouped into a service?
How do you enforce the Dependency Rule? Without tooling, the architecture drifts within 3 months.
items.a:
A rule that lives only in people's heads [[r:will drift]] — a new dev adds `import javax.persistence` to the domain and nobody catches it in review. Three levels of enforcement, increasing in strength: **1. ArchUnit — a test like any other, cheapest, do this first:** 
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.acme.booking")
class ArchitectureTest {
    
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domain_does_not_depend_on_infrastructure =
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAnyPackage("..adapter..", "org.springframework..",
                                "jakarta.persistence..", "com.fasterxml..");
    
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule layers_respect_direction =
        layeredArchitecture().consideringOnlyDependenciesInLayers()
            .layer("Domain").definedBy("..domain..")
            .layer("Application").definedBy("..application..")
            .layer("Adapter").definedBy("..adapter..")
            .whereLayer("Adapter").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
            .whereLayer("Application").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Adapter");
    
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_field_injection_allowed =
        noFields().should().beAnnotatedWith(Autowired.class);
}
**2. Maven/Gradle module** — `domain` is a module that declares no dependency on Spring/JPA at all. The compiler blocks it instead of a test; in exchange the build gets more complex and cross-module refactors get slower. **3. Spring Modulith** — `ApplicationModules.of(App.class).verify()` checks module boundaries inside a monolith, and also generates documentation and diagrams (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q8). [[g:Practical recommendation]]: ArchUnit from day one (10 lines, runs in CI), split into modules only once the team is large and the rule keeps getting violated. :::deep - Put ArchUnit in [[o:mandatory CI]], not an optional test. A rule that doesn't run in the pipeline is a rule that doesn't exist. - Start with [[g:a single rule]] (domain doesn't depend on infrastructure) and tighten gradually. Applying 15 rules to an old codebase at once makes the team disable the whole test suite. - For a codebase with existing violations: ArchUnit has `freeze()` (`FreezingArchRule`) — it locks in current violations as a baseline and only blocks *new* ones. This is the only way to apply it to a project already in flight, and it's a very "actually done this" answer. - Rules worth adding early: forbid `System.out`, forbid `java.util.Date`, require class names in `port/in` to end with `UseCase`, forbid cycles between packages (`slices().should().beFreeOfCycles()`). - ArchUnit reads bytecode, so it [[r:cannot]] catch dependencies through reflection or class-name strings — rare, but worth knowing the limitation. - Tooling still needs to run alongside review: dependencies pointing the right way while business logic sits in the wrong place is something no tool catches. :::

items.q: Which layer should transactions, validation, and mapping live in?
items.a:
Three things that cut across layers, and getting them wrong is a common reason an architecture with "the right folders" is still hard to maintain. **Transaction — in `application/service`, exactly one place.** - [[g:Use case = one transaction]]. Opens on entry, closes on exit. - [[r:Don't]] put `@Transactional` on the controller (holds the transaction open through JSON serialization) and [[r:don't]] put it on the repository adapter (each call becomes its own transaction → the use case loses atomicity). - The domain [[g:must not know]] what a transaction even is — it's an infrastructure detail. **Validation — three kinds, three different places:**
KindExampleLives inReturns error
Syntacticwell-formed email, positive number, required fieldadapter/in (@Valid on the web DTO)400
Domain invariantcan't cancel an already-issued ticketdomain409/422
Rule needing external datais the seat still free, is the balance sufficientapplication (read via port, then ask the domain)409
A domain invariant [[o:must]] live in the domain, even if the adapter already checked it — the adapter can be bypassed (Kafka consumer, batch job, test), the domain cannot. **Mapping — each layer maps into the layer inward from it, never skipping layers:** 
WebRequest ──(adapter/in)──> Command ──> Domain
Domain ──> Result ──(adapter/in)──> WebResponse
Domain <──(adapter/out)──> JpaEntity
:::deep - `@Transactional` on a `private` method or called internally via `this` [[r:doesn't run]] — Spring's proxying (03-spring-boot-deep-build.ioc-container-transactions.q4). This is a classic bug, and in this architecture it tends to show up when a use case gets split into small methods within the same class. - Calling an external API (PSP, GDS) [[r:must not]] happen inside a DB transaction (18-query-optimization.rewriting-the-query-reshaping-the-model.q4): it holds the connection open for the entire network wait. Correct pattern: a short transaction writes `PENDING` status → call external system → a short transaction writes the result, or use an outbox (topic 9). - Any invariant [[o:that can't]] be protected in memory (preventing double-booking across multiple instances) has to fall back to a DB constraint or an atomic update — this is the real boundary of Clean Architecture, and being able to explain it scores well (16-project-concurrency-whiteboard.presenting-dissecting-the-ota-project.q2). - `@Valid` only checks shape. Don't stuff business rules into a custom validator — they'll end up outside the domain and unreusable. - Mapping across many layers looks excessive for CRUD, so for a simple context [[g:deliberately allow a shortcut]] and record the decision (an ADR) instead of rigidly applying it everywhere. :::

items.q: How does the test pyramid map onto the layers? Why does Clean make testing cheaper?
items.a:
The most pragmatic reason to choose Clean is [[o:not]] "cleanliness" but [[g:fast, stable tests]] — answering with this hits the real point.
LayerTest kindToolingSpeedProportion
Domainpure unit, no SpringJUnit + AssertJ~1msthe most
Application (use case)unit with fake portsJUnit + fake/mock~5msa lot
Adapter out (DB)narrow integration@DataJpaTest + Testcontainers~1smoderate
Adapter in (web)narrow integration@WebMvcTest~1smoderate
Full systemmain happy paths@SpringBootTest~10svery few
ArchitecturerulesArchUnit~2s1 suite
**Why it's cheaper:** the domain doesn't import Spring, so testing it [[g:needs no context to start up]]. A 2000-test domain suite runs in a few seconds. In a layered codebase where logic sits in `@Service` calling `Repository` directly, every test has to spin up a context or mock JPA — slow and brittle. 
// Testing the use case: the port is an interface so it can be faked, no DB needed
@Test void cannot_hold_a_seat_someone_else_already_holds() {
    var locks = new InMemorySeatLocks();       // hand-written fake, not Mockito
    locks.tryLock("VN231", "12A");              // someone else holds it first
    var service = new HoldSeatService(new InMemoryBookings(booking), locks);
    
    var r = service.hold(new HoldSeatCommand(id, "VN231", "12A"));
    
    assertThat(r.status()).isEqualTo(TAKEN);
}
:::deep - [[g:Hand-written fakes beat mocks]] for a port used a lot: `InMemoryBookingRepository` written once, used in 50 tests, is easier to read than 5 lines of `when(...).thenReturn(...)`. Mocks are fine for a single call. - [[r:Anti-pattern number one]]: `@SpringBootTest` for everything. The suite takes 8 minutes to run, developers stop running tests locally, and tests fail for reasons that have nothing to do with what they're testing. - Testcontainers [[g:beats H2]]: H2 has no next-key locking, different syntax, a different query plan — tests pass while prod fails. This is a place worth being strict about. - Domain tests should be named after the [[o:business rule]] (`cannot_cancel_an_already_issued_ticket`) rather than the method (`testCancel`). Reading the test list reads like a spec. - This architecture also makes [[g:consumer-driven contract testing]] (17-rest-api-design.contracts-errors-lifecycle.q4) natural: the web adapter is thin, so contract tests only need to touch the adapter. - Measure with [[o:mutation testing]] (PIT) if you want to know whether tests actually catch bugs — high coverage with a low mutation score means tests exercise the code without actually checking anything. :::

items.q: How do you migrate a running layered codebase to Clean, step by step?
items.a:
This question separates people who read about it from people who've actually done it: [[r:nobody gets to rewrite from scratch]]. Do it incrementally, staying deployable at every step.

**A deliberate order — 6 steps:**

1. **Pick the single most painful bounded context** (usually Booking or Payment), not the whole repo. Win in one place before spreading out.
2. **Build a safety net first**: characterization tests for current behavior. Without tests, every refactor is a gamble.
3. **Extract `port/out` first** — this is the highest-payoff step. Create a `BookingRepository` interface in `application/port/out` and have the existing `JpaBookingRepository` implement it. No need to change the model or add a mapper yet.
4. **Pull business rules out of `Service` and down into the domain**, one rule at a time. Each pull adds a pure domain test.
5. **Split use cases** out of the `BookingService` god-class: each public method becomes its own use case class.
6. **Split the model** (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q2) — [[o:do this last]], since it's the most effort for the least payoff. Many teams stop at step 5, and that's good enough.

**Guarding against drifting back:** turn on ArchUnit with `freeze()` starting at step 3 — lock in old violations as a baseline, block new ones (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q4). Without it, new code keeps getting written the old way while you're cleaning up the old code.

:::warn Common mistake
Starting by [[r:creating all 4 folders and dumping the old classes into them as-is]]. The result is layered wearing a Clean costume: folders are right, dependencies are still wrong, and the team believes it's done. The dependency direction is the architecture, not the folder tree.
:::

:::deep
- Apply the [[g:strangler fig]] pattern: write *new* features in the new structure right away, migrate old features when there's a reason to touch them anyway. No sprint ever gets approved for "pure refactoring" — so it has to ride along with real work.
- Step 3 has the highest payoff because it [[o:unlocks testing]]: having an interface means you can fake it, which means you can write tests fast, and every later step depends on that.
- Measure progress with numbers: how many classes in `domain` don't import Spring, how many tests need no context, how long the suite takes to run. Saying "it's cleaner now" doesn't get you approval to keep going.
- Write an [[g:ADR]] (Architecture Decision Record) for big decisions — six months later even you will have forgotten why you chose to split the model.
- For legacy systems integrated externally, insert an [[o:Anti-Corruption Layer]] (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q6) at the boundary so their messy model doesn't seep into the new domain.
- Know when to [[r:stop]]: a purely CRUD context only needs steps 1–3. Forcing Clean onto a lookup module is exactly the over-engineering 12.4 warns about.
:::

items.q: Package-by-layer vs package-by-feature, and Spring Modulith for a modular monolith?
items.a:
**Package-by-layer** (the default for most Spring projects): 
com.acme
├── controller/   BookingController, FlightController, UserController
├── service/      BookingService, FlightService, UserService
└── repository/   BookingRepository, FlightRepository, UserRepository
Opening the repo only tells you *"this is a Spring app"*. Changing one feature touches 3 folders, and [[r:nothing stops]] `UserService` from calling `BookingRepository` directly. **Package-by-feature** (also called [[o:screaming architecture]]): 
com.acme
├── booking/      web/ · application/ · domain/ · persistence/
├── flight/       web/ · application/ · domain/ · persistence/
└── user/         web/ · application/ · domain/ · persistence/
Opening the repo tells you right away *what this system does*. More importantly: `booking` can keep everything except its public API [[g:package-private]] — the compiler blocks cross-access, no tooling needed. **Spring Modulith** — turns that boundary into something checkable: 
@Test void modules_respect_boundaries() {
    ApplicationModules.of(Application.class).verify();     // fails on a violation
}
// Modules communicate via events, not by calling each other's beans directly
@ApplicationModuleListener                            // = async + transactional
void on(BookingConfirmed e) { notifications.send(e.bookingId()); }
It also generates module diagrams and documentation straight from the code, and has an event publication registry so events aren't lost when a consumer fails. :::deep - The two axes are [[o:independent]]: layer vs. feature is *how you split packages*; Clean/Hexagonal is *dependency direction*. The best combination is feature on the outside, layer on the inside (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q1). - A modular monolith is the right stopping point for most teams (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q5): clear boundaries without paying the distributed-systems cost. Split into micro-services when there's an [[g:operational reason]] — uneven scaling, different release cadences, separate teams — not just for "cleanliness". - Modules communicating via [[g:domain events]] instead of calling beans directly is the best preparation for splitting services later: switching from in-process events to Kafka barely touches business code. - Spring Modulith by default treats [[o:each direct subpackage of the root package]] as a module, and only what's at the module's top level counts as its public API — this convention is what keeps it lightweight. - Don't split modules by technical layer (`web`, `db`) — split by business capability. A shared `persistence` module is a distributed monolith in miniature (12-architecture-patterns.patterns-principles.q3). - Getting the split wrong is still fixable while it's a monolith; getting it wrong after splitting into micro-services is very expensive. That's why [[g:modular monolith first, split later]] is almost always the right advice. :::
